Getting Started — Core Engine

getting-started.Rmd

What is aRtifacts?

aRtifacts is a schema-agnostic observability engine for tabular data. If your data lives in a data.frame and you can name the columns that make each row unique, aRtifacts can snapshot it, diff it, and run quality rules against it — regardless of whether it’s clinical, financial, operational, or anything else.

This vignette walks through the core engine using a plain, made-up dataset so you can see the mechanics without any domain-specific jargon.

Step 1 — Create a domain snapshot

A domain snapshot is an immutable capture of one table at one point in time. You tell it the table name, hand it a data.frame, and declare which columns form the unique key.

library(aRtifacts)

# Imagine a simple orders table.
orders_v1 <- data.frame(
  order_id   = c(101, 102, 103),
  customer   = c("Alice", "Bob", "Carol"),
  amount     = c(250, 480, 120),
  status     = c("shipped", "pending", "shipped"),
  order_date = c("2025-06-01", "2025-06-03", "2025-06-04"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

snap_v1 <- new_domain_snapshot(
  name     = "orders",
  data     = orders_v1,
  key_vars = "order_id"
)

What just happened? new_domain_snapshot() validated that order_id exists in the data and that every row has a unique value. If either check fails, you get an immediate error — no silent corruption downstream.

Step 2 — Make a second snapshot and diff

Now suppose a new extract arrives: one order amount was corrected, a new order was added, and an existing order was removed.

orders_v2 <- data.frame(
  order_id   = c(101, 103, 104),
  customer   = c("Alice", "Carol", "Dave"),
  amount     = c(250, 135, 310),
  status     = c("shipped", "shipped", "pending"),
  order_date = c("2025-06-01", "2025-06-04", "2025-06-10"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

snap_v2 <- new_domain_snapshot(
  name     = "orders",
  data     = orders_v2,
  key_vars = "order_id"
)

Key diff — who was added or removed? 

diff_keys(snap_v1, snap_v2)
#> $added
#>   order_id
#> 3      104
#> 
#> $removed
#>   order_id
#> 2      102

added shows order 104 (Dave) appeared. removed shows order 102 (Bob) disappeared. This is purely key-level — it doesn’t look at values.

Value diff — what changed on matching rows? 

diff_values(snap_v1, snap_v2, vars = c("amount", "status"))
#>   order_id    var old new
#> 2      103 amount 120 135

Carol’s amount moved from 120 → 135. Only rows that exist in both snapshots are compared; added/removed rows are handled by diff_keys().

Step 3 — Bundle into an artifact snapshot

An artifact snapshot groups one or more domain snapshots together with build metadata (like a Git SHA or a run ID). This is useful when you have multiple related tables that move together.

art_v1 <- new_artifact_snapshot(
  domains     = list(orders = snap_v1),
  build_id    = "pipeline-run-041",
  code_sha    = "abc123",
  inputs_hash = "hash_v1"
)

art_v2 <- new_artifact_snapshot(
  domains     = list(orders = snap_v2),
  build_id    = "pipeline-run-042",
  code_sha    = "abc123",
  inputs_hash = "hash_v2"
)

diff_meta_artifact(art_v1, art_v2)
#>                     field              old              new changed
#> spec_version spec_version             <NA>             <NA>   FALSE
#> data_cut         data_cut       2026-02-23       2026-02-23   FALSE
#> build_id         build_id pipeline-run-041 pipeline-run-042    TRUE
#> code_sha         code_sha           abc123           abc123   FALSE
#> inputs_hash   inputs_hash          hash_v1          hash_v2    TRUE

The metadata diff tells you which build properties changed between two runs. Here the build_id and inputs_hash changed but code_sha stayed the same — meaning the code didn’t change, but the data did.

Step 4 — Write and run a flag rule

A flag rule is a small function that receives a data.frame and returns the rows that violate some condition. You wrap it in new_flag_rule() so the engine tracks its ID, severity, and ownership.

rule_high_amount <- new_flag_rule(
  id         = "HIGH_AMOUNT",
  domain     = "orders",
  severity   = "warning",
  category   = "business_logic",
  owner_team = "Finance",
  fn = function(df) {
    flagged <- df[!is.na(df$amount) & df$amount > 300, , drop = FALSE]
    if (!nrow(flagged)) return(data.frame())
    flagged[, c("order_id", "customer", "amount"), drop = FALSE]
  }
)

flags_v1 <- run_flags(art_v1, list(rule_high_amount))
flags_v2 <- run_flags(art_v2, list(rule_high_amount))

run_flags() applies every rule to its target domain inside the artifact and returns a single combined table of all flagged rows, annotated with RULE_ID, SEVERITY, and OWNER_TEAM.

flags_v1
#>   order_id customer amount     RULE_ID DOMAIN SEVERITY       CATEGORY
#> 2      102      Bob    480 HIGH_AMOUNT orders  warning business_logic
#>   OWNER_TEAM
#> 2    Finance
flags_v2
#>   order_id customer amount     RULE_ID DOMAIN SEVERITY       CATEGORY
#> 3      104     Dave    310 HIGH_AMOUNT orders  warning business_logic
#>   OWNER_TEAM
#> 3    Finance

Step 5 — Track flags over time

diff_flags() compares two flag tables and classifies each finding as introduced (new), resolved (gone), or persisting (still there).

diff_flags(flags_v1, flags_v2, by = c("order_id", "DOMAIN", "RULE_ID"))
#> $introduced
#>   order_id customer amount     RULE_ID DOMAIN SEVERITY       CATEGORY
#> 3      104     Dave    310 HIGH_AMOUNT orders  warning business_logic
#>   OWNER_TEAM
#> 3    Finance
#> 
#> $resolved
#>   order_id customer amount     RULE_ID DOMAIN SEVERITY       CATEGORY
#> 2      102      Bob    480 HIGH_AMOUNT orders  warning business_logic
#>   OWNER_TEAM
#> 2    Finance
#> 
#> $persisting
#> [1] order_id   customer   amount     RULE_ID    DOMAIN     SEVERITY   CATEGORY  
#> [8] OWNER_TEAM
#> <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

Bob’s high-amount flag was resolved (his row is gone). Dave’s is introduced (new row with amount > 300). This is how you track data-quality trends across pipeline runs or data cuts.

What’s next?

The core engine shown above works with any keyed tabular data. SDTM and ADaM checks are available as bundled supplemental modules — see the companion vignettes:

  • SDTM Module — snapshot and check SDTM domain tables
  • ADaM Module — validate ADSL, BDS, and explore the core rule catalog

You can also build your own domain-specific rule packs for any schema by following the same new_flag_rule() + run_flags() pattern shown above.
